strengths: Practical application: Generating transparent (RGBA) video is highly relevant and valuable for video editing, game development, and digital compositing.

Efficient design: Embedding the alpha channel into the native latent space of Wan-VAE enables the reuse of the base diffusion transformer and allows seamless integration with existing acceleration frameworks (e.g., LightX2V for 4-step generation without CFG).
Data curation: The paper demonstrates that a carefully filtered and captioned dataset of modest size (437 samples) can effectively adapt a strong foundational video model to RGBA generation.
Visual fidelity: Qualitative examples show clean edges, semi-transparency handling, and compelling details (such as hair and translucent liquids) in comparison to the baselines.
weaknesses: Absence of quantitative evaluation: The experimental section contains no quantitative metrics. There are no standard video generation metrics (e.g., FVD, CLIP text-video alignment), no quantitative VAE reconstruction benchmarks (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, or alpha SAD/MSE), and no structured human evaluation/user study.

Unfair qualitative comparison: In Figures 10–16, baseline models (TransPixeler open/close) are prompted with brief generic text (e.g., 'A parrot flying.', 'A coin spinning.'), whereas the proposed method uses heavily engineered, detailed prompts (e.g., 'This video has a transparent background. A vibrant tropical parrot soars, wings spread. Close-up. Realistic style.'). This makes it difficult to decouple the benefits of the architecture from prompt engineering.

Complete lack of ablation studies: The paper introduces several design choices—such as the causal 3D convolution merge block, composite losses (Sobel edge, perceptual, soft/hard rendering), and DoRA vs. LoRA—yet provides no ablation experiments to validate their individual contributions.

Limited methodological novelty: The overall conceptual approach directly adapts LayerDiffuse and AlphaVAE principles to the Wan backbone using standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/DoRA) and causal 3D blocks already native to Wan-VAE.
Incomplete manuscript details: Key parts of the submission appear unfinished, such as the missing project link in the abstract ('available on our website: .').

strengths: Practical and relevant application: Generating high-quality RGBA videos with alpha transparency is an impactful problem with direct utility in gaming, VFX, and content editing.

Efficient latent-space design: Reusing the pre-trained diffusion transformer latent space via a feature merge block and low-rank adaptation avoids duplicating the backbone network (unlike dual-branch architectures such as TransPixeler), allowing efficient 4-step inference and compatibility with existing acceleration pipelines.

Promising qualitative synthesis: Visual examples demonstrate plausible handling of challenging transparent and semi-transparent visual elements, including liquid, glass, smoke, and fine details such as hair strands.
Transparent discussion of limitations: The paper openly illustrates common failure modes, including alpha map holes and unintended background artifacts in complex scenes.
weaknesses: Complete absence of quantitative evaluation: The experimental evaluation contains no quantitative metrics (such as FVD, CLIP text-video alignment scores, VBench, or standard matting/reconstruction metrics like MSE/SAD on validation sets), nor any structured human evaluation or user study.

Unfair baseline prompt comparison: In Figures 10–16, TransPixeler is evaluated on extremely short prompts (e.g., 'A parrot flying'), whereas Wan-Alpha receives heavily engineered prompts enriched with detailed descriptions, stylistic tags, and shot sizes (e.g., 'This video has a transparent background. A vibrant tropical parrot soars, wings spread. Close-up. Realistic style.'). This disparity confounds model capability with prompt engineering.

Lack of ablation studies: The paper does not provide ablation experiments to validate the individual design choices, such as the utility of the Sobel edge loss, the necessity of both soft and hard rendering objectives, the causal 3D merge block vs. simpler concatenation, or the empirical benefit of DoRA over standard LoRA.

Limited methodological novelty: The underlying methodology largely adapts the paradigm established by LayerDiffuse to a modern video foundation model (Wan), combining standard causal 3D convolutions with parameter-efficient fine-tuning without significant algorithmic advances.

Questionable open-domain generalization: The text-to-video DiT module is fine-tuned on only 437 curated samples for 1,500 iterations. Without systematic benchmarking across unseen open-domain prompts, it is unclear whether the model retains broad generalizability or primarily reproduces templates close to its limited training distribution.

strengths: Practical and modular framework: By encoding transparency into the existing RGB latent space through a causal 3D convolution feature merge block and low-rank adaptation (LoRA/DoRA), the method preserves the pre-trained diffusion model architecture without duplicating backbones or significantly increasing inference overhead.

Efficient generation pipeline: Successfully integrates rapid 4-step sampling (via LightX2V) without classifier-free guidance, achieving fast generation speeds for high-frame-rate videos (81 frames at 16 FPS).

Well-designed VAE training objectives: The combination of hard-rendering, soft-rendering, Sobel edge supervision, and perceptual losses enables the VAE to retain fine details (e.g., hair strands, edges) and semi-transparent effects (e.g., glass, glowing particles, smoke).
Promising qualitative demonstrations: The visual samples show high-fidelity alpha mattes and smooth motion across various challenging transparency cases.
weaknesses: Complete absence of quantitative evaluation: The paper does not provide any quantitative metrics (such as FVD, FID, CLIP score, VBench, or standard matting metrics like SAD/MSE on the validation split). The evaluation relies entirely on qualitative visual comparisons across a few cherry-picked examples.

Unfair and uncontrolled baseline comparisons: Comparisons against TransPixeler are heavily confounded. First, TransPixeler is built on CogVideoX-5B, whereas Wan-Alpha uses the newer and significantly more capable Wan backbone; without controlling for the underlying base model, it is unclear how much gain comes from the proposed RGBA strategy versus the superior RGB foundation model. Second, the test prompts are mismatched (e.g., short, sparse prompts for TransPixeler vs. long, detailed, style-tagged prompts for Wan-Alpha in Figures 10–16).

Lack of ablation studies: There are no ablation experiments to substantiate key technical decisions, such as the causal 3D merge block vs. simpler 2D/3D fusion, the impact of soft/hard rendering loss formulations, the utility of the Sobel edge loss, or the performance difference between DoRA and standard LoRA.

No user study: Given the purely subjective claims regarding visual quality, motion consistency, and transparency realism over prior art, a structured human perceptual evaluation is necessary but missing.

Limited dataset scale and questionable generalization: The diffusion model is fine-tuned on only 437 samples (301 videos, 20 images, 116 internet clips). While fine-grained manual annotation is commendable, there is insufficient empirical analysis to demonstrate that the model generalizes robustly across broad text distributions without overfitting.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in generative video modeling: high-quality RGB-A video synthesis with accurate transparency, fine details (e.g., hair, semi-transparent smoke/glass), and temporal consistency.

The overall architectural formulation is computationally elegant. By encoding RGB and alpha into a shared latent space and using LoRA/DoRA adapters rather than duplicating the backbone DiT (as done in prior works like TransPixeler), the model maintains inference efficiency and leverages base model capabilities, achieving significant speedup (15x faster generation via 4-step sampling).

The transparency-guided mean sampler introduces an intuitive mechanism for both training stabilization and test-time controllability, allowing users to guide foreground positioning and scale via an ellipse prior.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation, including VBench metrics, GPT-4o evaluations, user studies, and component ablations, demonstrates superior qualitative and quantitative performance over previous RGB-A video baselines.
weaknesses: Mathematical and optimization justification for the bidirectional diffusion loss ($L_{bidiff} = M \cdot L_{RF}$ with $M = -1$ on transparent regions) is underspecified. Minimizing a negative squared error loss is unbounded below and typically leads to gradient explosion or divergence; the paper should clarify how stability is ensured (e.g., gradient clipping, weighting, or bounded activations).

The DiT fine-tuning dataset is notably small (only 429 samples). Although low-rank adaptation helps prevent overfitting, relying on such a limited set raises questions regarding open-domain generalization across diverse multi-subject and complex action prompts.

The single Gaussian ellipse prior assumes a unimodal, roughly convex spatial distribution of the foreground. For multi-object scenes or disjoint foreground elements, this parametric assumption may be overly restrictive or provide inaccurate spatial guidance.

strengths: Practical and timely problem: Generating RGB-A videos with high-fidelity transparency and semi-transparency is valuable for video editing, visual effects, game design, and UI asset creation.

Well-motivated architecture: Keeping latent dimensions compatible with the base text-to-video foundation model (Wan2.1) via lightweight adapters (LoRA/DoRA) avoids duplicating the entire diffusion backbone, enabling high inference efficiency and compatibility with few-step distillation techniques like LightX2V.

Controllability via noise space mean-shifting: Using a Gaussian ellipse prior in the noise space provides an intuitive, training-free mechanism for users to roughly guide foreground scale and positioning during inference.

Comprehensive qualitative demonstrations: The paper demonstrates strong visual quality across difficult semi-transparent cases such as smoke, fire, lighting, and fine structures like fur and hair, outperforming standard two-stage generation + video matting pipelines.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison across different base models: The proposed method is built upon Wan2.1-T2V-14B, an exceptionally strong open-source video foundation model. In contrast, several baselines (e.g., AnimateDiff+LayerDiffuse, LayerFlow, TransPixeler) rely on smaller or older backbones. It is unclear how much of the performance advantage in Table 1 (e.g., aesthetic quality, text alignment, motion smoothness) stems from the proposed framework versus the substantially stronger generative prior of the 14B base model.

Theoretical and stability concerns regarding the bidirectional diffusion loss: Eq. (3) negates the Rectified Flow loss for non-opaque regions ($M(p) = -1$). Performing unconstrained gradient ascent on an MSE loss can easily cause numerical instability or push latent vectors to extreme values unless heavily constrained by reconstruction terms. The paper lacks formal analysis, gradient bounds, or discussion on hyperparameter sensitivity regarding this inverted objective.

Unimodal assumption in Gaussian ellipse modeling: The noise mean sampler estimates a single 2D Gaussian ellipse via principal component analysis of the binarized alpha mask. This assumption breaks down in multi-subject scenes, non-convex shapes, or complex topologies with disjoint foreground regions.

Small-scale fine-tuning data for the DiT: The DiT is fine-tuned on only 429 samples (301 video clips, 43 images, 85 internet clips). Although DoRA limits the trainable parameter space, training on fewer than 500 samples raises concerns regarding semantic generalization, prompt drifting, and dataset memorization across open-domain prompts.

Insufficient user study and evaluation details: Table 2 reports average ranking, but the paper does not specify essential experimental protocols, including the number of human participants, the total prompt pool size, whether raters were experts or crowd workers, and whether observed differences are statistically significant.

strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and practically important problem in video generation: synthesizing high-fidelity RGB-A videos with stable transparency and semi-transparent effects without degrading the base model's generative capacity.

The technical design is creative and well-motivated. The transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss (TABD) cleverly leverages a frozen DiT to steer latent representations, preserving familiar RGB latents while separating alpha latents.

The transparency-guided mean sampler is an elegant mechanism that regularizes transparent background synthesis during rectified flow training while inherently providing users with spatial and scale controllability during inference.

The proposed method achieves substantial improvements over existing state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., TransPixeler, LayerFlow) across text alignment, aesthetic quality, and temporal consistency, while achieving notable inference acceleration (15x faster generation using 4-step sampling).
Ablation studies clearly substantiate the individual contributions of the rendering losses, TABD, and the mean sampler.
weaknesses: The bidirectional diffusion loss applies an inverted sign ($M = -1$) to transparent and semi-transparent latents, effectively performing gradient ascent on the rectified flow objective. The paper does not provide sufficient theoretical or empirical analysis regarding how gradient ascent is bounded to prevent latent explosion or training instability during VAE learning.

For standard unconditional/text-only inference, the model defaults to placing a centered Gaussian ellipse. The paper lacks discussion on how well this default prior handles prompts describing multiple objects, background-filling elements, or scenes requiring off-center compositions.

The fine-tuning dataset for DiT RGB-A video generation is relatively small (429 samples). Although training via DoRA helps retain the base model's knowledge, a deeper discussion or ablation on the generalization limits across diverse unseen categories and open-domain text prompts would be valuable.

The quantitative evaluation renders RGB-A onto a plain white background to run VBench and GPT-4o metrics. Including standard matting metrics (e.g., SAD, MSE, or Grad on alpha channels) on a paired held-out benchmark would provide a more direct, quantitative assessment of alpha matte boundary fidelity.
